docs.title: Owned analog selector navigation
docs.text:
See Lobby and Existing Canvas for normal authored navigation. This advanced API is useful for custom selector presenters.

InputNavigationGate converts one input owner's Vector2 callbacks into intentional selector steps. Create one gate per route, feed both performed and canceled callbacks into Read, and poll Repeat with the same monotonic time source. Dispose/reset the gate when its route is released. The character-selection lobby template and standalone persistent selector use unscaled Unity time.

Default InputNavigationSettings:

  • Activation threshold: 0.6 on the dominant axis.
  • Release threshold: 0.3; hysteresis prevents noise from generating new steps.
  • Initial repeat delay: 0.35 seconds.
  • Repeat interval: 0.16 seconds, with at most one step per poll.

Crossing activation generates one immediate step. Center release rearms it. A clear direction reversal generates an immediate new step; a partial reversal cancels repetition in the old direction. Repeated analog callbacks do not themselves advance the selector. Keyboard and D-pad input retain immediate discrete behavior without these repeat timers.

IsAnalog recognizes sticks, including joystick sticks, and excludes keyboard keys and D-pad controls. Settings are exposed on each presenter integration; timer/latch state is owned by each session route, never by PlayerIndex or a global controller.

docs.title: Character Catalog and Previews
docs.text: A Character Catalog is your ordered collection of selectable CharacterDefinition assets. Each definition has a stable Character ID, a display name, Gameplay Prefab and optional preview/portrait settings. Catalog order controls browsing, not identity. Begin with Quick Start; configure lobby UI with Chapter 5 — Lobby Templates and Existing Canvas.

docs.title: Create or choose a catalog
docs.text:
1. Open Tools > LevelArgento > Couch Co-op Builder > Character Catalog Generator, or Generate from Prefabs... in the Wizard's Characters step.
  2. Add your playable prefab assets using Add Slot or Add Selected Prefabs. Choose an existing Output Folder under Assets.
  3. Choose Create a new Character Catalog and its name, or assign Existing Catalog to append eligible definitions.
  4. Review Plan lists creation/reuse decisions and any blocking problems. Generate Reviewed Assets creates the reviewed definitions/catalog without modifying source prefabs or overwriting existing assets. Saved disk assets are not guaranteed to reverse with Undo.
  5. Assign the resulting catalog to the Wizard, or select an existing catalog in its Character Catalog field. Inspect its definitions and use Run Catalog Validation before testing selection.

You can also create Character Catalog/Character Definition assets from Unity's Create > Couch Co-op Builder asset menu and assign definitions manually. Keep Character IDs nonempty and unique. Renaming display names or reordering entries need not change IDs; changing an ID breaks existing references to that selection. Reuse the established ID when updating a definition.

docs.title: Validation and selection state
docs.text:
Use a nonempty catalog with no null/duplicate entries, blank/duplicate IDs or missing Gameplay Prefabs. The built-in lobby selection requires that valid catalog even when your gameplay later binds existing objects or uses a custom provider. The Wizard may allow Apply with a missing-prefab warning; assign those prefabs before expecting lobby confirmation to succeed.

If an ID no longer exists, is ambiguous or its catalog is missing, the gameplay context reports unresolved character metadata instead of inventing a substitute. Correct the definitions/catalog, validate, and select again. API-only gameplay metadata lookup does not require a prefab; selected-character spawning does. See Gameplay Integration for that distinction.

SelectedCharacterId belongs to the joined session and persists through lobby/gameplay transitions until permanent Leave. Ready belongs to the lobby scene and resets on reconstruction. Preview focus, committed selection and Ready are separate: browsing/moving focus alone does not commit a Character ID or clear Ready. Confirm commits the choice; external committed-selection/catalog changes can invalidate Ready.

docs.title: Preview host
docs.text: CharacterPreviewHost is a scene-local runtime presenter. It accepts a CharacterDefinition, creates a presentation-only clone, frames its child renderers, and exposes a small RenderTexture suitable for any lobby view.

docs.title: Public API
docs.text:
• Show(CharacterDefinition) displays or replaces the active definition.
  • RefreshPresentation() recalculates framing without replacing the clone.
  • Clear() releases the clone, camera, light, RenderTexture, and runtime layer lease.
  • SetOutputSize(width, height) adjusts the bounded 64-1024 pixel output.
  • ActiveDefinition, ActiveInstance, OutputTexture, FallbackPortrait, DisplayMode, and StatusMessage expose current presentation state.
  • PresentationChanged lets a layout update its prefab, portrait, or placeholder view.

The host does not know about player sessions, input, Ready state, scene loading, or a specific lobby layout.

docs.title: Prefab and fallback resolution
docs.text:
The host uses CharacterDefinition.SelectionPreviewPrefab. That property resolves an explicit preview prefab first and otherwise returns the gameplay prefab. If neither is available, or if the resolved prefab has no child Renderer, the host exposes the definition's portrait. When no portrait exists, DisplayMode.Placeholder preserves the character name and a reason through the consuming view.

MeshRenderer, SkinnedMeshRenderer, SpriteRenderer, and other Renderer subclasses are discovered on all children. An Animator is optional. Its controller's default state plays normally; Preview Settings > Animation State can request an existing state without requiring a humanoid rig or a LevelArgento-specific controller.

docs.title: Framing
docs.text: All child renderer bounds are combined, including off-center children. Perspective framing accounts for texture aspect ratio and expands when an animated pose exceeds the original bounds. Per-character settings provide position, rotation, scale, framing padding, and an optional Animator state/layer. These adjustments affect only the runtime clone.

docs.title: Camera and resource isolation
docs.text:
Each active host owns one disabled camera, directional light, and 256x256 RenderTexture. The camera renders manually only while that host's renderers are temporarily enabled. The host automatically leases an unused, unnamed runtime layer rather than requiring a fixed project layer or changing TagManager settings. Other preview hosts remain disabled during that render, so player previews cannot render each other's instances. The camera never reads or modifies the customer's Main Camera.

The host releases all native and scene objects on Clear, disable, destruction, Leave, and scene teardown. It does not create a camera or texture per catalog entry.

docs.title: Gameplay prefab fallback limitations
docs.text:
A gameplay prefab can contain scripts, input components, physics, audio, or other match-only behavior. The host instantiates it beneath an inactive runtime root, disables all cloned MonoBehaviours, physics collisions/simulation, and play-on-awake audio before activating the clone, and leaves Animator components available.

Unity invokes a cloned MonoBehaviour's Awake during Instantiate before the host can disable that component. OnEnable, Start, and later callbacks remain suppressed, but gameplay prefabs with unsafe Awake logic are not suitable as direct preview fallbacks. Other component-specific initialization can also have side effects. Assign a dedicated SelectionPreviewPrefab when a gameplay prefab is expensive, depends on gameplay services, or contains behavior that should never exist in a lobby. The source prefab and its assets are never modified.

docs.title: Lobby integration
docs.text: The supplied lobbies create one preview host per joined panel. Browsing changes only that host's presentation. Confirming uses CharacterSelectionService to commit SelectedCharacterId and set scene-local Ready. Leave clears the departing panel's preview; returning to the lobby reconstructs it without replacing the session or InputUser. See Lobby and Existing Canvas for authored view assignments.

docs.title: Configure Supplied Samples
docs.text: ProjectSettings are not shipped with the asset. Multi-scene samples load their Lobby, Arena or return scene by name, so opening the first scene alone does not register its destinations for your project.

docs.title: Preview and explicitly apply
docs.text:
1. In Edit Mode, open Tools > LevelArgento > Couch Co-op Builder > Configure Supplied Samples.
  2. Select Rocket Rumble 2D, Rocket Rumble 3D, Persistent Sessions, or Select All Samples.
  3. Review the target shown at the top and the Scene list after configuration preview.
  4. Click Configure Selected Samples. No project configuration changes happen on import or merely by opening the window.
  5. Open the selected sample's first scene below and enter Play Mode.
Sample Scenes, in configured order Rocket Rumble 2D RocketRumble2DMainMenu, RocketRumble2DLobby, RocketRumble2DArena Rocket Rumble 3D RocketRumble3DMainMenu, RocketRumble3DLobby, RocketRumble3DArena Persistent Sessions PersistentLobbyPrototype, PersistentGamePrototype

The first scene in each row is its entry scene. Rocket Rumble scene assets are under Samples/RocketRumble2D/Scenes/ and Samples/RocketRumble3D/Scenes/; Persistent assets are under Prototypes/Persistent/, all relative to Assets/LevelArgento/CouchCoopBuilder/. The Sample Index gives complete entry paths.

Split Screen Playgrounds have an independent join/gameplay flow within their own scenes. They do not need this multi-scene configuration simply to enter Play Mode.

docs.title: Unity 6 Build Profiles and shared scenes
docs.text:
When the active Build Profile has Override Global Scenes enabled, the tool updates that profile's scene list. Otherwise it updates EditorBuildSettings.globalScenes, the shared scene list used by profiles without overrides. The target label states which list will change. Other profiles are not edited.

Only the selected samples' scenes are enabled, deduplicated and grouped in the order shown. Their block replaces the first selected-scene occurrence, or is appended if none was present. Unrelated scenes keep their relative order, enabled state and GUID. Existing sample scenes and product assets are not modified.

Running the same selection again produces the same scene list. It is safe to rerun after reviewing the target. Missing scene assets are reported and prevent applying; configuration is unavailable during Play Mode.

docs.title: Reverting
docs.text: Profile changes support Unity Undo. Revert Last Configuration can restore either target list while the window remains open and that same target list still matches the applied configuration. If another edit changes the list, Revert is disabled rather than overwriting that edit. Shared scene-list changes use this Revert action rather than Unity scene Undo. Review Build Profiles separately from scene-file saves.

docs.title: Built-in Focus and Navigation
docs.text: Couch Co-op Builder contains its own focus and navigation implementation for the Setup Wizard, supplied lobbies, Rocket Rumble menus and Split Screen Playgrounds. It works without another LevelArgento product. The separate Smart UI Focus & Navigation product is not included and is not required.

docs.title: Player-owned focus
docs.text:
PlayerFocusManager controls one assigned EventSystem. In a multiplayer panel it uses that player's MultiplayerEventSystem and input module; it never substitutes another player's global EventSystem. The Wizard creates and connects these components automatically in the Existing Canvas workflow.

PlayerFocusScope defines the selectable region. On scope assignment the manager selects a valid remembered control, the default selection, or a valid descendant, in that order. Disabled, inactive, non-interactable and out-of-scope controls cannot receive focus. Clear remembered selection when opening a panel that should always start on its default control.

docs.title: Modals and input modes
docs.text:
The sample menus push a modal scope for binding capture and reset confirmation. Closing a modal returns to the prior scope/control when still valid, or recovers a valid selection. Destroyed objects and unavailable EventSystems are tolerated during teardown.

PlayerUiInputModeDetector observes only the actions assigned to its owned InputSystemUIInputModule. Keyboard/controller interaction permits automatic focus recovery. Pointer mode avoids immediately reclaiming a mouse-cleared selection. It does not create input users, pair devices, enable other players' actions or change Join/Leave behavior.

docs.title: Navigation groups and overrides
docs.text: UiNavigationGroup generates explicit directional links for the small authored Playground panels. It excludes inactive/non-interactable controls and controls belonging to a nested group. UiNavigationOverride can direct an edge to a particular valid control or intentionally leave it unlinked. Existing explicit links elsewhere, including the per-player lobby and Rocket Rumble menu routing, remain authored by those workflows.

docs.title: Samples
docs.text: Study lobby templates and Existing Canvas, Rocket Rumble menus, and Split Screen Playgrounds. The built-in module is product-specific; it does not include the standalone product's inspectors, layout constraints, showcases, documentation or branding.

docs.title: Installation and updates
docs.text: The module lives under Assets/LevelArgento/CouchCoopBuilder/Runtime/UI/FocusNavigation/ and uses the Couch-owned LevelArgento.CouchCoopBuilder.UI assembly. Keep it with Couch. No standalone-product installation or compatibility fingerprint is needed. Back up customer-authored scenes and scripts before updating Couch.

docs.title: Lobby input and controller profiles
docs.text:
Lobby Join/Leave/Navigate/Confirm belong to the shared input services and scene UI presenters; configuring a gameplay action asset does not rebind them. Default lobby controls provide two logical keyboard roles plus recognized gamepads. Additional hardware needs a matching profile and usable controls, not merely a device visible in Input Debugger.

For a generic joystick or supported HID exposed through a Joystick-derived layout, create a GenericControllerProfile and assign it to Shared Joystick Input → Profiles. Add Couch Co-op Builder > Joystick Control Discovery temporarily to a scene object, enable Diagnostics Enabled, enter Play Mode and operate the device to inspect reusable control paths in Console, then configure Join, Leave, Confirm, Cancel and navigation. Keep a specific base layout/interface and exact hardware metadata filters. Reported HID VID/PID select the controller type; manufacturer/product provide the configured fallback when required HID IDs are unavailable. A reported HID mismatch is rejected rather than bypassed by text matching. Avoid a broad layout-only profile unless that scope is intentional.

One reusable profile can match identical controllers. Runtime device/display names (including appended numbers) do not identify physical hardware. The most specific matching profile is selected; ties are ambiguous and need corrected configuration or an explicit runtime profile assignment. Each joined device still gets independent actions, InputUser and session. Type/profile matching is not proof of unique physical identity across launches; saved overrides use Input Binding Profiles.

docs.title: Gameplay input binding
docs.text:
Resolution chooses which object represents the player. Input mode chooses how that object consumes the authoritative session's input. Configure them separately:

Input strategy is independent of representation mode. A resolved object can use Built-in Actions, PlayerInput Adapter or Custom Adapter when configured for that strategy. API Only can consume the context directly without a representation binding.

Configure GameplayPlayerBinding on the prefab or existing object. Its default is Handle Input Myself, so gameplay input evaluation remains opt-in. Runtime owners can call binding.ConfigureInput(mode, settings, existingPlayerInput, adapter) after resolution. Changing configuration explicitly releases the old input cycle. Inspector changes apply on the next binding cycle.

docs.title: Four input strategies
docs.text:
1. Handle Input Myself: no gameplay actions, PlayerInput creation or gameplay method calls. Use Context.TryGetInputUser and read PairedDevices, Slot, PlayerIndex and SessionId directly. API-only resolution requires no binding at all. No missing-settings error is emitted.
  2. Built-in Actions: assign GameplayInputSettings, which references a customer-owned InputActionAsset and map names for Keyboard A, Keyboard B, Gamepad and Joystick. The selected map provides Move/Look (Vector2) and PrimaryAction/SecondaryAction/Jump/Pause (Button). Those names/types are the built-in adapter contract; use Custom Adapter for another contract. Each player gets a clone, including runtime binding overrides; only its selected map is enabled. Access binding.Input and its actions or ActionTriggered. No movement, physics or camera behavior is included.
  3. PlayerInput Adapter: a limited, explicit bridge for an already-authored PlayerInput using native Unity Events. See the limitations below. PlayerInput is never required or automatically added.
  4. Custom Adapter: assign a MonoBehaviour implementing IGameplayInputAdapter, or pass a plain interface instance to ConfigureInput. TryBind receives the real Context and existing GameplayPlayerBinding. Unbind is called once when that input cycle ends, including rollback after TryBind fails/throws. Make Unbind safe after partial initialization. Use one adapter instance per representation; sharing one live instance is rejected. Custom code owns its created resources and must clean them up.

The binding's Context is the only authoritative player association. Input setup follows context assignment. Awake/OnEnable may precede binding, especially on a spawned prefab. Subscribe to InputBound for context plus input readiness; inspect IsInputReady/InputFailure. ContextChanged is emitted after the initial input attempt; it does not guarantee a successful optional adapter. Scene systems can use GameplayPlayerSetup.PlayerResolved, then inspect input readiness. Late consumers replay the current binding state. Input failure leaves the valid representation/context in place, logs player/session details and raises InputBindingFailed; it does not silently change input strategy or prevent other players from binding.

docs.title: Session ownership and keyboard roles
docs.text:
The built-in evaluator does not create an InputUser, pair devices or call AssociateActionsWithUser. The installed Input System supports one associated action collection per user: replacing it would reset the persistent lobby map's device/mask filtering. Instead, gameplay clones maintain explicit device lists from the existing user's paired devices and subscribe to InputUser/device changes. An empty list is kept explicit; it never becomes the null/all-devices fallback. Session availability and pairing govern map enabling. There are no per-frame searches, action cloning or input allocations in this evaluator.

Keyboard A/B intentionally share a physical keyboard and have distinct session users. Device filtering alone cannot separate them. As with the existing lobby architecture, they use two explicit, disjoint logical action maps. Both maps are validated against the owned keyboard: resolved controls must be individual keys and must not overlap across roles. Full-keyboard/wildcard/mouse bindings and missing/equal role maps are rejected. Align customer gameplay role maps with the customer's lobby roles; editing a lobby template does not automatically remap the separate gameplay asset. The supplied defaults use the established WASD/F and Arrow/Enter role controls, plus distinct gameplay-only buttons.

Gamepad maps evaluate only their session's paired device(s), independent of Gamepad.current, Gamepad.all ordering or device display names. Built-in Joystick maps optionally use Context.JoystickProfile, the profile actually assigned to that session. Move reuses its directional bindings, processors and effective layout paths. Optional Gameplay controls on GenericControllerProfile customize Look/Primary/Secondary/Jump/Pause. Empty Primary/Secondary/Pause use Confirm/Cancel/Join respectively; empty Look/Jump remain unbound. Leave remains the existing profile Leave control. Identity matching and join policy are unchanged. Turn off Use Joystick Profile in GameplayInputSettings to use a customer-authored joystick map instead. PlayerInput mode uses its authored action bindings rather than rewriting native action IDs.

Lobby and gameplay have separate action instances and callbacks. Disposable lobby presenters/UI modules unsubscribe on scene exit. Persistent session maps continue managing the existing Join/Leave/reservation behavior; they are not forwarded into gameplay and are not replaced with a new associated collection. A physical key/button can have an intentional meaning in each scene. Avoid assigning gameplay actions to existing Leave controls unless Leave is intended.

docs.title: PlayerInput bridge: support and limitations
docs.text:
The installed PlayerInput exposes a read-only user and automatically creates/pairs its own user in OnEnable. There is no public API to adopt the existing session user or set its native playerIndex. This bridge never enables PlayerInput's native lifecycle and uses no private-field reflection or Input System modifications.

Requirements:

  • Author PlayerInput disabled, on the same gameplay object as GameplayPlayerBinding, before it can be instantiated/activated. Built-in spawning rejects opted-in input prefabs with enabled PlayerInput components before Instantiate. An already-enabled component is incompatible; the adapter cannot undo auto-pairing that customer initialization already performed.
  • Select Invoke Unity Events. Its existing persistent action events are retained and installed on the isolated cloned asset through the public actions getter.
  • Assign a source action asset that is not enabled elsewhere; the bridge rejects an enabled source instead of disabling someone else's actions.
  • Do not assign a UI Input Module. The bridge owns gameplay action evaluation only.
  • Keep the gameplay object active while using the bridge. Deactivation releases its clone; activation begins a fresh input cycle.

The bridge temporarily assigns the cloned asset/current map to the runtime PlayerInput, preserves default map/control scheme/camera/notification/event configuration, and restores the original asset on release. Shared keyboard uses explicit KeyboardA/KeyboardB maps, validated as above. With optional GameplayInputSettings, its map names select the player's map; otherwise controller roles use PlayerInput.defaultActionMap. Only the selected gameplay map is enabled.

Native PlayerInput.user/devices/playerIndex remain invalid/empty/-1. The originating session's InputUser, paired devices and PlayerIndex remain unchanged and are exposed through GameplayPlayerBinding.Context. Native active-player registration, PlayerInputManager, automatic control schemes, SwitchCurrentActionMap and native device-lost/regained notifications are not supported by this bridge. Use Context availability and the owned Input.Map instead. Do not enable PlayerInput or call ActivateInput/SwitchCurrentControlScheme while bound.

Send/Broadcast Messages and native C# onActionTriggered are deliberately rejected: the installed PlayerInput gates those paths on its private input-active state. Native Unity action events do not have that gate and can be safely wired without a second user. C# consumers can instead subscribe to binding.Input.ActionTriggered or use Built-in/Custom adapters. This is a UnityEvent compatibility bridge, not adoption of the canonical user into PlayerInput.

docs.title: Lifetime, live joins and failures
docs.text:
Input bindings follow representation binding, release, deactivation and scene teardown. Owned action maps are disabled/disposed, all framework callbacks are unsubscribed, native UnityEvent hooks are removed and the original PlayerInput asset is restored. Customer objects/source assets are not destroyed. Custom Unbind exceptions are diagnosed without stopping other players' cleanup. Do not retain an Input instance after release.

A live join binds input once when its representation resolves. The built-in spawner still waits for its first character selection. An intentional Leave releases only that player's gameplay input/object; survivors keep indexes/users/instances. Device Lost disables unavailable owned actions but retains the same session, object and adapter. The existing services restore ownership on reconnect; device/user notifications update filtering without creating another user, callback set or representation. Your game owns reconnection feedback and pause policy.

Missing settings/assets/maps/actions, wrong built-in value types, keyboard overlap, incompatible PlayerInput configuration and custom adapter exceptions are isolated input failures. Unexpected object destruction also releases input through the existing binding lifecycle and resolution diagnostic. Explicit reconfiguration or deactivation/activation starts a new input cycle; failures are not retried every frame.

docs.title: Minimal custom adapter
docs.text:
The public factory is also useful when custom code wants the standard isolated evaluator. The returned object is owned by the caller, who must Dispose it. Other custom adapters may consume Context directly instead.

using LevelArgento.CouchCoopBuilder;
using UnityEngine;
using UnityEngine.InputSystem;

public sealed class MyGameplayAdapter : MonoBehaviour, IGameplayInputAdapter
{
    [SerializeField] private GameplayInputSettings settings;
    private GameplayActionInput input;

    public bool TryBind(GameplayPlayerContext context,
        GameplayPlayerBinding binding, out string failureMessage)
    {
        input = GameplayActionInput.Create(context, settings);
        input.ActionTriggered += OnAction;
        failureMessage = null;
        return true;
    }

    private void OnAction(InputAction.CallbackContext callback)
    {
        if (callback.performed) { /* Consume this player's action. */ }
    }

    public void Unbind()
    {
        if (input == null) return;
        input.ActionTriggered -= OnAction;
        input.Dispose();
        input = null;
    }
}

See Input Binding Profiles for runtime rebinding and profile-based persistence. Lobby controls, gameplay controls and saved profile identity are separate concepts.

docs.title: Gameplay Representation and Spawning
docs.text:
Quick Start covers the initial lobby workflow. This guide explains gameplay context, object ownership, input and session lifecycle for 1–8 players. Joining/selection do not prescribe how your game represents a player; spawn points and PlayerInput are optional.

Representation mode Choose it when Spawn Selected Character The confirmed Character Definition supplies a Gameplay Prefab that Couch should instantiate and clean up. Bind Existing Objects Characters, vehicles or other representations already exist in the scene; bind each authored object by Player Index. Custom Provider Your pool, team/grid or creation system chooses and owns a live object for each context. Handle It Myself / API Only Your architecture consumes the public contexts and manages its own representations. No object setup is required.

Resolution chooses the object; input configuration separately chooses how it consumes owned controls. Your game supplies movement, physics, scoring and match rules. Shared Camera and Split Screen is an optional module for assignment/viewports; your game supplies camera follow/framing. No Couch base class or prefab inheritance is required.

docs.title: Scene setup
docs.text:
Add Couch Co-op Builder > Gameplay Player Setup to a scene object. Set Mode in the Inspector. Bootstrap may be explicitly assigned; otherwise the component uses CouchCoopBootstrap.Active. Initialize the bootstrap before enabling the setup (automatic execution order accommodates a normally initialized persistent bootstrap).

For Handle It Myself, the component creates and binds no gameplay objects and requires no object array/provider. The component itself is optional when your game only uses the public context API.

For Bind Existing Objects, assign an object at each required zero-based array index. Index 0 belongs to P1, index 7 to P8, independent of object names or hierarchy. Objects must belong to the setup's scene. The framework adds/reuses GameplayPlayerBinding and assigns its Context; it preserves transforms, parents and active state. Unused authored objects remain unassigned with their authored active state, including objects authored inactive. It does not activate/deactivate, instantiate or destroy them. Your game controls visibility and gameplay lifetime.

For Custom Provider, assign a MonoBehaviour implementing IGameplayPlayerProvider. Runtime code can alternatively call Configure(mode, authoredObjects, provider, bootstrap) with a plain interface implementation. This is a small example; replace the indexed decision with your own pool, vehicle or team logic:

using LevelArgento.CouchCoopBuilder;
using UnityEngine;

public sealed class MyGameplayProvider : MonoBehaviour, IGameplayPlayerProvider
{
    [SerializeField] private GameObject[] authoredVehicles;

    public bool TryResolve(GameplayPlayerContext context,
        out GameObject playerObject, out string failureMessage)
    {
        playerObject = context.PlayerIndex < authoredVehicles.Length
            ? authoredVehicles[context.PlayerIndex] : null;
        failureMessage = playerObject != null ? null : "No vehicle assigned to this player index.";
        return playerObject != null;
    }
}

The provider receives the persistent context including character metadata and input ownership. It returns one live scene GameObject (never a prefab asset), or returns false with an explanation. Resolution attempts occur when sessions enter the enabled setup; repeated Initialize() does not retry failures or repeat successful calls. Rejoin after reversible Drop Out requests a fresh association for the same session. Disable/re-enable or call Configure to begin a new resolution cycle. Explicit lifecycle owners can call Release() and then Initialize(). Never assume the framework will retry or instantiate a fallback. Two active contexts cannot bind the same object. The provider owns creation and reclamation; subscribe to PlayerReleased if it needs to return objects to a pool.

Read GameplayPlayerBinding.Context on a resolved object, or use setup.TryGetPlayerObject(playerIndex, out object) from a scene system. Consumers may subscribe to ContextChanged, where null means released. Composition is optional for API-only integrations and requires no base-class inheritance or PlayerInput. Character changes update the live context and do not automatically replace the resolved gameplay object.

docs.title: Notifications and lifetime
docs.text:
• GameplayPlayers.PlayerAdded / PlayerRemoved: joined/left context. Subscribe, then replay Players for existing sessions.
  • GameplayPlayers.SelectionChanged: selection/catalog notification. Built-in spawning uses the first selection of a waiting live join; existing representations are not replaced.
  • GameplayPlayerSetup.PlayerResolved / PlayerReleased: scene object association/release. Subscribe before Initialize if you need initial replay notifications.
  • GameplayPlayerSetup.ResolutionFailed: failure for that context; also logged with player index and session ID.

Unsubscribe scene-owned consumers in OnDisable. The setup unsubscribes before teardown and clears its scene references on disable/destroy; bindings clear their Context without reconstructing UI. Destroying a bound object releases the association immediately and reports a useful error on the next surviving setup frame. Deferring that diagnostic avoids false errors during ordinary scene unloading. The bootstrap stores no resolved objects, so scene reload gets fresh bindings and one provider call per joined session per visit.

Existing live Join creates a context and resolves it if a scene setup is enabled. Leave removes its context and releases its binding. Built-in owned instances are destroyed; customer-owned Existing/Custom objects are preserved. An explicit rejoin creates a new session and resolves the available index. Physical input loss keeps existing reservation semantics and does not rerun a provider. These are association semantics only: gameplay scoring, match participation, respawn and pool reclamation remain customer responsibilities. The optional reversible Drop Out policy preserves the session while releasing scene bindings. See Gameplay Input Integration for optional input adapters.

Missing indexed bindings, missing/destroyed providers, false/null provider results, provider exceptions and conflicting object ownership report isolated failures. Other players continue resolving; there is no fallback strategy. Use character-resolution status/message for optional metadata failures. No scene-wide searches or per-frame hierarchy scans are used. Destruction detection checks at most eight cached object/binding references per setup frame, covering never-active objects whose Unity OnDestroy callback may be skipped; diagnostics process a bounded pending queue.

docs.title: Spawn Selected Character
docs.text:
Spawn Points and PlayerInput are optional. This gameplay representation mode requires GameplayPrefab; Existing Objects, Custom Provider and API Only do not. The separate built-in lobby selection rule above still requires valid prefabs.

Choose Spawn Selected Character on GameplayPlayerSetup, then one placement strategy. Runtime owners can call ConfigureSpawning(placement, points, origin, offset, placementProvider, bootstrap).

  1. Explicit Spawn Points: assign zero-based indexed Transforms. PlayerIndex 5 uses element 5 even when other sessions have left. World position/rotation come from that Transform; its scale does not affect the prefab. Missing/destroyed required points fail only that index; there is no reuse or world-zero fallback.
  2. Origin + Offset (Single Origin And Offset): assign one Origin Transform and Per Player Offset. Position is origin.position + origin.rotation * (offset * PlayerIndex); rotation is origin.rotation. Offset is expressed along the origin's local axes in world units; origin scale is ignored. With an unrotated origin at (10,1,5) and offset (2,0,0), P1 is (10,1,5), P2 is (12,1,5), P3 is (14,1,5). Rotating the origin rotates the formation. XY offsets support 2D, XZ offsets support 3D. An origin is required; there is no implicit world-zero placement.
  3. Custom Placement Provider: assign a MonoBehaviour implementing IGameplaySpawnPlacementProvider. Runtime configuration also accepts a plain interface implementation. The provider receives the real context and returns a world Pose; it never needs to create the character or implement IGameplayPlayerProvider. Each attempted spawn calls it once. A false result/exception/invalid pose affects only that player.
using LevelArgento.CouchCoopBuilder;
using UnityEngine;

public sealed class MyPlacement : MonoBehaviour, IGameplaySpawnPlacementProvider
{
    [SerializeField] private Transform gridOrigin;
    public bool TryGetSpawnPose(GameplayPlayerContext context,
        out Pose pose, out string failureMessage)
    {
        pose = default;
        failureMessage = null;
        if (gridOrigin == null)
        {
            failureMessage = "Assign the grid origin.";
            return false;
        }
        Vector3 offset = new Vector3(context.PlayerIndex * 3, 0, 0);
        pose = new Pose(gridOrigin.position + gridOrigin.rotation * offset,
            gridOrigin.rotation);
        return true;
    }
}

The selected ID resolves through GameplayPlayerContext against the current catalog. Only the definition's GameplayPrefab is instantiated. Missing/ambiguous character IDs or a missing prefab fail with the existing ResolutionFailed event and diagnostic. SelectionPreviewPrefab and portrait are never gameplay fallbacks. The source prefab is never changed. Root scale and active state remain prefab-authored; placement supplies world position/rotation. A compatible GameplayPlayerBinding is reused, otherwise added to the runtime clone only. Clones are moved into the setup's scene even when another additive scene is active.

docs.title: Ownership and live sessions
docs.text:
Built-in clones are framework-owned. Release, component deactivation, Leave and scene teardown unbind and destroy only those clones. PlayerReleased fires after unbinding and before destruction is scheduled; normal Play Mode Destroy completes at frame end. A disabled setup removes its built-in representations; re-enabling starts a fresh cycle. Existing and Custom Provider objects remain customer-owned and are never destroyed by this cleanup.

No additional InputUser is created, no pairing is performed and no action maps are switched. Physical Device Lost keeps the reserved session and its existing object; the live context reports input unavailability. Reconnection does not duplicate or respawn it. An intentional middle-player Leave destroys only that player's built-in instance and leaves survivors' indexes and transforms unchanged.

A live Join normally has no character selection: the built-in mode waits quietly for its first selection notification. That selection attempts one spawn. Existing joined sessions replayed at scene entry require a selection and report missing metadata as configuration failure. Failed attempts are not automatically retried; selection/catalog notifications do not repeat placement calls for an attempted context. To retry after correcting configuration, disable/re-enable, call ConfigureSpawning, or Release then Initialize. A character change after successful spawning updates the context but does not replace its representation; your game must implement respawn or mid-match character switching explicitly. Unexpected runtime destruction is released and diagnosed, with no automatic respawn.

The persistent bootstrap never stores clones. Resolution is driven by scene initialization, Join and the first selection of a waiting Join. Update checks only up to eight cached associations for destruction; it performs no catalog resolution, instantiation or global scene search.

docs.title: Customer initialization timing
docs.text:
Unity Instantiate can invoke prefab Awake and OnEnable before Context assignment. Do not assume context is available in either callback. Use the existing GameplayPlayerBinding.ContextChanged notification on a prefab that already contains that component, or GameplayPlayerSetup.PlayerResolved. ContextChanged guarantees the binding's Context; PlayerResolved additionally means the setup lookup has been registered. Subscribe before enabling/initializing setup if you need all initial resolutions. A late consumer can replay contexts and TryGetPlayerObject instead.

For a prefab with an existing binding, Awake may subscribe to ContextChanged; unsubscribe in OnDestroy using Unity's binding != null check. A prefab without a binding should use a scene-level PlayerResolved consumer because the binding is added after Instantiate. Use these notifications rather than relying on prefab initialization order. Use the optional gameplay input strategies below for action ownership; movement remains customer-owned.

docs.title: Installation
docs.text:
Use Unity 6.3 LTS, Unity Input System, and Unity UI (uGUI / TextMeshPro). The supplied visual and game samples use the Universal Render Pipeline (URP). Install the Unity Registry packages through Package Manager and enable the Input System in Player Settings. Core session, input, lobby and gameplay integration is not inherently tied to URP. Couch-owned focus and navigation are built in.

Before opening UI samples in a fresh project, use Window > TextMeshPro > Import TMP Essential Resources. Unity UI supplies the TMP APIs; this separate import supplies the default fonts, materials, shaders and TMP Settings used by the examples. Couch does not bundle those standard resources. If compatible Essential Resources are already present, keep them and your TMP configuration; do not overwrite them unnecessarily. No TMP Examples & Extras import is required. This is a one-time customer setup step.

docs.title: Quick Start
docs.text:
1. Open Setup Wizard. Choose Create New Lobby for an editable supplied presentation, or Integrate Existing Canvas for your own saved UI.
  2. Characters: assign a Character Catalog and Maximum Local Players. Use Generate from Prefabs... if you have no catalog: add your playable prefab assets, choose an existing Assets folder, Review Plan, then Generate Reviewed Assets. Assign the resulting catalog back in the Wizard.
  3. Lobby UI: choose a supplied style, an existing customer-owned Assets folder and a new asset name. For Existing Canvas, assign its shared Start Button and the required controls for each player.
  4. Gameplay: choose your saved Gameplay Scene, enabled in the project scene configuration. Open Gameplay Scene Additively lets you inspect its Gameplay Player Setup. Configure representation and input on those existing components using Chapter 7 — Gameplay Representation and Spawning and Chapter 8 — Gameplay Input Integration. API-only consumers can use their own game integration.
  5. Cameras: leave management disabled to keep your cameras, or Enable Shared / Split Screen Camera Management and assign the required gameplay references. Your game supplies camera follow/framing; see Chapter 10 — Shared and Split Screen Cameras.
  6. Review and test: resolve blocking issues, review output paths, scene-file changes and project scene-list changes, then Apply Setup. Use Open Lobby Scene, save, and Test Lobby in Play Mode. Join, choose characters, confirm every joined player, then submit the shared Start Game control.

The Wizard copies a supplied scene/prefab or wires your Existing Canvas. It configures the catalog, capacity and gameplay destination; optional camera wiring uses an existing gameplay setup. It does not create gameplay movement or configure input adapters. Save existing lobby/gameplay scene edits after Apply. Scene wiring supports Undo; created assets and project scene-list changes must be reviewed separately when reverting.

docs.title: Default lobby controls
docs.text:
Source Join Browse characters Confirm Leave Keyboard A Q A / D F G Keyboard B P Left / Right Enter Backspace Gamepad Start Left stick / D-pad South face button Select / Share / Create Generic joystick / supported HID Controller Profile Join Profile navigation Profile Confirm Profile Leave

Down moves focus toward shared Start in the supplied lobbies (S for Keyboard A, Down for Keyboard B). Moving UI focus does not clear Ready. Start requires at least one joined player, all joined players Ready, and their input available; Rocket Rumble additionally requires two players. Two logical keyboard roles share one physical keyboard. More players need compatible controllers. Gameplay controls are configured separately and can differ from lobby controls.

docs.title: Input Binding Profiles and Rebinding
docs.text:
See Quick Start for lobby setup and Gameplay Integration for owned action binding.

This opt-in runtime API belongs to Couch Co-op Builder. A game such as Rocket Rumble can build its settings UI on top of it. The framework does not create a controls menu, change existing Join/Leave listeners, or rebind the fixed UI navigation actions. It changes the owned gameplay action clones exposed by GameplayActionInput. Source InputActionAssets and GenericControllerProfile assets are not rewritten.

docs.title: Identity and shared profiles
docs.text:
PlayerIndex is a reusable session seat displayed as P1–P8; it remains stable until permanent Leave. InputSlot separately identifies the reserved input role/source, and SessionId is stable for that session. None is a persistent binding-profile key. Editing "P3 Controls" means editing playerBinding.Input.BindingProfile, the input source currently assigned to P3. After Leave, the next occupant receives its own source's profile.

Source Default persistent identity Consequence Keyboard A KeyboardA Follows the logical A role across seat changes. Keyboard B KeyboardB Follows the logical B role across seat changes. Standard gamepad Gamepad:Profile: plus a metadata family fingerprint Same reported family shares saved overrides. Xbox and DualSense families do not inherit each other's overrides through seat reuse. Generic joystick Joystick:Profile: plus the matched GenericControllerProfile identity fingerprint Uses the actual discovered profile; identical devices share that profile.

Gamepad family metadata includes the Unity layout, interface, manufacturer, product and HID VID/PID when reported. Display names, runtime device names, InputDevice.deviceId and serial numbers are not used as unique identity. A serial field alone is not evidence of cross-launch stability or uniqueness. A transport or layout change can select a different family fallback; this is a default/shared profile, not a claim of physical-device identity.

For generic joysticks, assign PersistentBindingProfileId once in the profile Inspector, or ConfigureBindingProfileId during configuration. Reuse that stable customer-owned ID when updating the profile asset. Existing assets with a blank ID use exact base-layout/interface/manufacturer/product/HID match fields. The fallback does not depend on asset/display names or generated binding GUIDs. Changing those match fields changes the fallback key. Use distinct explicit IDs for distinct profiles with otherwise identical match metadata.

Identical controllers cannot be reliably distinguished across launches by this fallback. They have independent actions, sessions and InputUsers, but share binding settings. Editing/resetting that shared profile updates every attached consumer of it. No fuzzy matching or invented physical identity is used.

A platform/customer integration with verified stable, unique physical identity can implement IInputBindingDeviceIdentityProvider and supply it to InputBindingProfileResolver. Returning true asserts both properties. Do not return a transient deviceId, enumerated display name, player seat, or unverified serial. Verified gamepad keys survive metadata/transport changes; verified joystick keys remain scoped to their controller profile. The framework itself provides no cross-platform guarantee of unique physical identity.

docs.title: Service and storage
docs.text:
Keep one InputBindingProfileService for the game's controls settings lifetime, usually across scene transitions. It owns one complete versioned document in an IInputBindingProfileStore. The core model has no dependency on UI or PlayerPrefs.

JsonFileInputBindingProfileStore is the simple built-in desktop/mobile backend. Its default file is Application.persistentDataPath/CouchCoopBuilder/input-bindings.json. An explicit file path is also supported. It writes a sibling temporary file and replaces the previous document. Customers can implement the two-method store interface using their own save system. Save must replace the whole document atomically, or throw without changing the previous document. Use one writer per store. Platforms without suitable filesystem support, including WebGL/cloud save integrations, should supply their own backend.

Load explicitly and handle a failure before exposing editing/resetting. A failed load retains the last successfully loaded document and live bindings. An empty or missing file means defaults. Unsupported versions, malformed data and duplicate records are rejected. Do not silently overwrite an unknown or unreadable save by continuing with defaults after a failed load.

var profiles = new InputBindingProfileService(new JsonFileInputBindingProfileStore());
if (!profiles.TryLoad(out string loadFailure))
{
    // Show/report loadFailure and stop editing until the save is resolved.
    profiles.Dispose();
    return;
}

// After an existing GameplayPlayerBinding has bound its input:
var playerProfile = profiles.Attach(playerBinding.Input);
bool saved = playerProfile.TryRebind(
    "PrimaryAction", 0, "<Gamepad>/buttonNorth", out string failure);

Attach after gameplay input is available, for example from the existing GameplayPlayerBinding.InputBound callback. Reattach to the new input when the scene representation is recreated. The service automatically detaches when that input is disposed and retains saved overrides. It never creates another InputUser or replaces InputUser.actions. Custom integrations can attach to their own GameplayActionInput.Create result and remain responsible for disposing it.

An input can have one binding profile session. A stable optional domain (default Gameplay) separates different customer action schemas in the same profile. Keep the domain stable across scenes using the same schema. Only the owned gameplay map is enabled/modified, not every map in the source asset.

docs.title: Settings before joining
docs.text:
profiles.OpenProfile(kind, gameplaySettings, device, joystickProfile) opens a settings preview using the same identity, storage, validation and reset operations. The returned InputBindingProfileSession.ActionMap is an owned, disabled clone for display and editing. It creates no PlayerSession, InputUser or synthetic device. Dispose the preview when changing profile or leaving settings. Later Attach(playerBinding.Input) consumes the saved overrides for that input source.

Both keyboard roles are validated in the preview even when nobody has joined. With no device, a preview can display defaults/saved data and reset, but cannot capture/rebind (CanRebind is false). A device-less gamepad preview represents the generic default Gamepad family; it is not a saved Xbox/DualSense physical identity. When a controller is connected, open its actual resolved family profile. Joystick previews require a configured GenericControllerProfile and use its identity, even when its device is absent. Connected joysticks must match that profile. SharedJoystickInput.ResolveProfile exposes the same strict discovery scoring and ambiguity result without enabling join listeners.

docs.title: Capture, paths and conflicts
docs.text:
The Rocket Rumble sample settings menu reserves Escape for keyboard capture only. Controller captures use the visible Cancel button or the ten-second timeout, leaving their ordinary UI Back/Cancel controls available as gameplay candidates. A controller-only user can wait for the timeout to abort without choosing a binding. This sample policy does not change the framework's optional cancelControl contract below.

var capture = playerProfile.BeginInteractiveRebind("PrimaryAction", 0);
capture.Finished += result =>
{
    // Inspect Status: Succeeded, Rejected or Canceled, and Failure on rejection.
    // Refresh UI here. Dispose/unsubscribe UI handlers when the menu closes.
};
// The UI's Cancel button or teardown calls capture.Cancel()/Dispose().

Only one capture can run per service. The target map is disabled during capture; other players' maps keep working. Capture accepts and suppresses only events from the target's paired devices. Runtime device paths restrict capture but are never saved. Other controllers and another player's Escape key cannot choose/cancel a binding. Cancel is explicit, or occurs at the default ten-second timeout, device loss/disable/unpair, input disposal, session disposal or service disposal. The operation releases native resources and restores the target map when its input is still available. The timeout is configurable. A caller can optionally supply cancelControl to BeginInteractiveRebind; it must belong to the selected source and uses Unity's existing native cancellation path. It is reserved for cancel during that capture, not saved as an override. Without it, cancellation remains explicit or by timeout.

Programmatic overrides must be a concrete layout-relative path such as <Keyboard>/h, <Gamepad>/buttonNorth or <Joystick>/button11. An empty string unbinds. Runtime instance paths and wildcard/usage paths are rejected. The path must resolve on the source's paired device and fit the action's expected control type. Rebind individual composite parts by binding index, not a composite header. Keyboard sources accept individual keys.

Keyboard A/B share one physical keyboard. The service validates both logical role maps, including the defaults/saved role that has not joined, and rejects cross-role overlap before saving or mutating live actions. Conflicting capture is reported as Rejected with a reason. Reuse by different actions in the same gameplay map is also rejected; multiple bindings of the same action are valid. Identical logical button paths on separate gamepads/joysticks are valid; they are not cross-device conflicts.

The consumer should close or otherwise gate its lobby controls while editing if captured keys also have existing Join/Leave/UI meaning. This foundation does not replace those listeners or implement a modal controls menu.

docs.title: Reset and action schema updates
docs.text:
• playerProfile.ResetAction(actionName, out failure) resets that profile/action in the current domain.
  • playerProfile.ResetProfile(out failure) implements Reset Player: reset the current source's persistent profile, across its domains and attached consumers.
  • profiles.ResetAll(out failure) clears all persisted framework profile overrides, including profiles with no currently attached player.
  • The service also exposes profile-based ResetAction/ResetProfile for settings screens that do not have a live player.

Reset restores the authored defaults captured at attachment, including any customer-authored template overrides, processors and interactions. It does not rewrite source assets. Changes validate using scratch maps and save before live maps change. A failed store save leaves live actions and the document unchanged. Finish/cancel capture before another mutation or reset. ProfilesChanged signals successful changes; PersistedProfileKeys lists profiles with saved overrides. All service operations are intended for Unity's main thread.

Binding addresses use action name and original structural binding information, not Unity-generated GUIDs (joystick actions are reconstructed with fresh GUIDs). If an action/binding schema changes, unmatched stored addresses are retained and listed in playerProfile.UnappliedBindings; they are not applied to a different binding. Plan an explicit customer save migration or reset for schema changes.

Dispose the service at application teardown. Dispose/cancel captures when their UI closes. Detaching a live session restores its owned map's defaults; disposing the underlying GameplayActionInput detaches without touching destroyed assets.

docs.title: Simultaneous action conflicts
docs.text: Profile validation rejects one physical control assigned to different actions in the selected gameplay map/domain, including composite parts and parent controls. Two bindings of the same action are valid. Both keyboard role maps are compared because they share a Keyboard. Separate controller devices are not compared. Lobby/UI maps and other binding domains are independent and may reuse controls. InputBindingProfileService.LastConflict exposes control display/path, both semantic action names and profile keys after a rejected transaction. Rejection leaves live bindings and storage unchanged. Authored defaults must also be valid for their simultaneously active map; resets are validated before saving.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
Couch Co-op Builder configures local multiplayer joining, independent lobby navigation, character selection and gameplay handoff for Unity uGUI and the Input System. Optional integrations provide owned gameplay actions, saved binding profiles and Shared Camera / Split Screen management. Your game supplies its UI design, gameplay rules, movement and camera follow behavior.

Start with Tools > LevelArgento > Couch Co-op Builder > Setup Wizard. Couch-owned focus and navigation are built in; no separate product is required.

docs.title: Player scope
docs.text:
Workflow / example Capacity Framework and Existing Canvas 1–8 local players; typically 2–8 for co-op Supplied authored lobby templates Up to 4 visual player slots Rocket Rumble 2D / 3D 2–4 players Split Screen Playgrounds 1–8 players

For five to eight lobby players, provide your own P1–P8 visual roots and use Existing Canvas. The Wizard wires those authored controls; it does not generate additional graphics. Both the lobby and your gameplay scene must accommodate the chosen capacity. More players/cameras require profiling your own content and hardware.

docs.title: Lobby Templates and Existing Canvas
docs.text: Use Tools > LevelArgento > Couch Co-op Builder > Setup Wizard to copy a supplied presentation or connect your own Canvas. Begin with Quick Start; Chapter 3 — Setup Wizard explains the current steps, outputs and saving. Couch-owned focus and navigation are built in.

docs.title: Supplied lobby presentations
docs.text:
Create New Lobby offers Individual Panels, Shared Stage and Character Carousel. Each has four authored visual slots; the Wizard disables unused slots for a smaller capacity. They use the same character-selection and shared Start services. Framework capacity is described in Player scope; Existing Canvas supports your own additional roots.

The copied scene/prefab belongs to your game. In Prefab Mode, edit anchors, positions, fonts, sprites, backgrounds and decorative behavior. Keep the functional binding references or assign your replacements. Use Prefab Variants where helpful. Keep your copy outside supplied paths so updates cannot replace your design.

docs.title: Existing Canvas
docs.text:
Choose Integrate Existing Canvas when you have a lobby design or need five to eight authored player panels. This is a supported setup path. Save the lobby scene first and author one complete root for each supported P1–P8 entry; object names and sample hierarchy names are not requirements.

The Wizard's Player panel dropdown displays the configured players. Fields marked * are required. Supply these references for each player:

Assignment Purpose / boundary Player UI Root Entire authored panel; one unique root per player on the assigned Canvas Choices Root Controls shown after Join; contained by that player's root Waiting State Root Your join prompt shown while the seat is empty; contained by that player's root Character Selector An authored Button inside Choices Root; one reusable selector browses the catalog Selector Label Either Legacy Text or TextMeshPro (TMP) beneath that player's root Preview Root Authored preview container inside the player's root Preview RawImage Displays the preview texture; inside Preview Root

Assign one authored shared Start Button on the Canvas. The Ready count label, focus highlight and per-player Start focus indicators are optional. Indicators can live elsewhere on that same Canvas; each assigned indicator belongs to one player.

Under Optional authored presentation, you may assign portrait/accent Images, focused/confirmed/previous/next character labels, identity/device/Ready labels, and Ready / Not Ready state roots. Optional previous/next labels are for custom presentations; the supplied carousel does not need them. Leave unused targets empty. Use one text implementation per role; TMP labels need an authored font.

Suggest unique components in this root only proposes references with exactly one candidate. It does not choose among multiple Buttons or RawImages. Review every suggestion and all required roots before applying.

docs.title: Input and navigation wiring
docs.text:
The Wizard adds/reuses nonvisual services and one independent input/focus/preview context per configured player. Each has its own MultiplayerEventSystem, InputSystemUIInputModule, PlayerFocusManager, PlayerUiInputModeDetector and PlayerFocusScope. The authored player root defines the player's UI boundary; the shared Start router is intentionally shared.

Advanced fields allow existing per-player EventSystems and preview hosts. Leave them empty to create missing components. Do not share the same EventSystem or input module between players. Keep each EventSystem with its input module in the saved lobby scene; its playerRoot must match that player's root. The Wizard reuses already-bound contexts on rerun.

Default lobby controls remain separate from gameplay input. Each player browses/confirms independently. Focused character previews and the committed selected Character ID are separate: browsing or moving UI focus does not itself commit a selection or clear Ready. Confirm commits the selected ID and sets Ready. Scene-local Ready resets when the lobby is reconstructed; intentional Leave clears the session's selection.

There is one shared Start Game action. Every joined session must be Ready and have available input; a reserved disconnected session blocks Start. Empty seats do not count. Start occurs only after an eligible player's submit, not automatically when the last player becomes Ready.

docs.title: Visual ownership and previews
docs.text:
Your prefab/Canvas owns all visible UI: layout, player roots, Buttons, labels, Images/RawImages, frames and backgrounds. Runtime code updates assigned content, preview textures, functional visibility/interactability and navigation. It creates no replacement visual hierarchy and does not restyle your layout. Surviving sessions keep their root through scene transitions; intentional Leave permits the lowest available Player Index to be reused.

The preview host owns scene-local rendering resources. Preview content prefers a Selection Preview Prefab, then Gameplay Prefab, portrait, and named placeholder. Dedicated presentation prefabs are recommended when gameplay initialization has side effects. See Character Catalog and Previews.

docs.title: Apply, extend and check
docs.text:
1. Choose Characters and capacity, then connect the saved Canvas and every required player entry.
  2. Choose the gameplay destination, optionally configure cameras, and resolve Review errors.
  3. Apply Setup, then save the lobby and any modified gameplay scene. Existing Canvas scene wiring supports Undo; Project scene-list changes are separate.
  4. Join and confirm independently; move focus to shared Start, enter gameplay, and return. Check that selection/identity persist, Ready resets, and authored layout remains yours.
  5. To extend later, author more complete roots, increase Maximum Local Players, assign the new entries and Apply again. Existing contexts are reused. Do not duplicate EventSystems manually just to rerun setup.

For API identity, object/input ownership and optional reversible Drop Out, see Gameplay Integration. For optional Shared/Split management, see Split Screen Cameras.

Figure 2. Character Carousel: four authored panels, independent selection and a shared Start control.

Figure 3. Shared Stage presents four independent player contexts together.

docs.title: Persistent Sessions
docs.text: This four-panel example demonstrates session/input ownership and selected Character IDs across lobby → game → lobby, with scene-local Ready. It is a UI/context example, not a movement, combat or production gameplay scene. See Player scope for framework capacity and Chapter 3 — Setup Wizard for setup.

docs.title: Open and run
docs.text:
Use Configure Supplied Samples to register Persistent Sessions. Open Assets/LevelArgento/CouchCoopBuilder/Prototypes/Persistent/PersistentLobbyPrototype.unity, then enter Play Mode. The sample creates one persistent bootstrap only when none exists. Join using default lobby controls; navigate each player's panel independently.

The lobby includes its own Persistent Sample Catalog (Assets/LevelArgento/CouchCoopBuilder/Prototypes/Persistent/PersistentSampleCatalog.asset), which reuses the shipped Astral Capsule and Neon Cube character definitions and preview prefabs. The character selector requires a valid catalog; replace the sample catalog on the lobby's PersistentScenePrototype with your own to browse different characters. Confirm each joined player, then focus START GAME and submit; the lobby requires all joined players Ready with available input. The game shows RETURN TO LOBBY, without a Ready label. Confirm it to return.

docs.title: What persists
docs.text:
Session ID, zero-based Player Index, input role/slot, InputUser and selected Character ID persist. Each session keeps its corresponding panel across scene transitions; gaps do not compact. Intentional Leave ends that session and frees its seat/slot. The next Join can use the lowest available seat; survivors retain theirs. Physical Device Lost keeps the existing reservation.

Ready is scene-local and resets when the lobby is reconstructed. Navigation changes preview focus only; confirmation commits selection and Ready. Returning reconstructs scene-local UI/previews while keeping authoritative sessions and users. The sample supplies a minimal camera when no enabled scene camera exists.

docs.title: Concepts to study
docs.text:
Read CouchCoopBootstrap, PersistentScenePrototype and the independent player presenters. A panel's Character Preview Host renders presentation content separately from gameplay. Gameplay Integration explains context APIs, representation ownership and advanced recovery.

Try two keyboard roles, then supported controllers: join/confirm independently, transition twice, Leave/rejoin a middle seat and compare surviving session/panel mappings. Test actual device loss separately from intentional Leave. Optional Report Persistent Session Diagnostics on the scene component prints ownership details when needed; verbose logging is off by default.

docs.title: Rocket Rumble 2D
docs.text:
An optional 2–4-player platform combat sample for Couch Co-op Builder, Unity 6.3 LTS, URP and Input System. It demonstrates selected-character spawning, isolated gameplay input, profile rebinding and persistent session flow. Its fixed Shared Camera, movement, combat and match rules are game content; framework scope is explained in Player scope.

Figure 4. Rocket Rumble 2D uses one fixed shared view and independent player combat actions.

docs.title: Open and play
docs.text:
Open RocketRumble2DMainMenu (Assets/LevelArgento/CouchCoopBuilder/Samples/RocketRumble2D/Scenes/RocketRumble2DMainMenu.unity), enter Play Mode and choose PLAY. Join at least two players, browse Cobalt/Ember/Mint/Orchid, confirm Ready and activate START GAME. First register its three scenes using Configure Supplied Samples. Customize your own copies of the supplied scenes, catalog and prefabs; keep RocketRumbleShared when using this sample.

Shared Rocket Rumble guidance covers Main Menu, Audio/Controls, Pause, Device Lost, Drop Out/Rejoin and scene returns. Lobby controls are separate from the gameplay controls below.

docs.title: Gameplay controls
docs.text:
Source Move Jump Fire Shield Pause / winner return Keyboard A A / D Space F Left Shift T Keyboard B Left / Right Numpad 0 Enter Right Shift Y Gamepad Left stick horizontal North South Left Trigger Start Supplied DragonRise profile Stick horizontal button3 button2 button1 button11

Join/Leave defaults are Q/G, P/Backspace, Start/Select and DragonRise button11/button12. Gameplay actions are independently rebindable; this game does not consume Look or vertical Move. Up/stick Up never jumps. One press requests one grounded jump; holding through landing does not jump again. Dead/countdown/winner states reject Jump without audio.

docs.title: Arena and jump
docs.text:
Rigidbody2D movement retains facing on release, including horizontal air control. Jump speed is 17.5, with body gravity scale 3 and airborne multipliers 1.4 rising / 2 falling. A floor jump reaches approximately 3.54 units, peaks around 0.40 seconds and lands around 0.76 seconds. The first platform is reachable; the center platform needs intermediate traversal. Solid undersides block upward passage, and side-wall contact is not grounding. Tune the supplied player prefabs for your game's scale.

Rockets fire horizontally with a 0.35-second cooldown, speed 18 and lifetime 2.5 seconds. They ignore their owner, consume on a valid hit and have no splash damage. One unblocked opponent hit causes one death and one attacker point; falling is an unscored death.

docs.title: Shield, respawn and match
docs.text:
Hold Shield to raise a frontal energy plate while moving/firing. Releasing without a block costs nothing. A frontal incoming rocket is consumed without death/score and starts a five-second cooldown; rear attacks bypass protection. A second rocket can kill after the shield is spent. HUD displays Ready, Active or remaining cooldown. Death/respawn resets Shield and requires a fresh press.

The authored 3 → 2 → 1 → GO! countdown blocks gameplay. Default first to 10 kills wins, with five-second respawn. The same object, context, InputUser, selection and score survive ordinary death/respawn. Eleven authored floor/platform points prefer at least five units from living opponents, avoid the previous point when possible, and otherwise maximize separation. Missing respawn points fall back to initial authored spawns.

Victory stops gameplay/scoring, clears rockets and displays the winner. Any joined player with available input can use their Pause shortcut or the pointer Return button to return to the originating lobby. Identity/selection persist; Ready and the next match's score reset. Reversible Drop Out instead releases/recreates the representation while keeping score; shared lifecycle guidance explains that distinction.

docs.title: Integration to study
docs.text:
• GameplayPlayerSetup: Spawn Selected Character + Explicit Spawn Points; the framework owns instantiation and scene cleanup.
  • GameplayPlayerBinding: context and Built-in Actions; the match consumes PlayerResolved / PlayerReleased and replays already-resolved objects.
  • RocketRumble2DPlayerController / RocketRumble2DProjectile: owned actions, physics, facing and combat.
  • RocketRumbleMatchController / RocketRumbleRespawnPoints / RocketRumbleHud: session-owned score, safe respawn, authored TMP feedback and match flow.
  • Shared menus and settings: included sample audio and framework Input Binding Profile integration.

This sample uses one fixed Shared Camera. Rocket Rumble 3D demonstrates runtime Split Screen; Split Screen Playgrounds demonstrate up to eight participants. The 2D game is not a generic movement, matchmaking or arbitrary-content performance solution.

docs.title: Try your integration
docs.text: Start with Q/P, confirm independently and move to Start without losing Ready. Move/jump/fire/shield independently, die and respawn, then return after victory. Change Fire to an unused key in Controls and confirm that lobby Confirm stays unchanged. Test Pause/Resume, Drop Out/Rejoin and physical Device Lost separately; repeat with your supported controllers and check Console on scene exit.

docs.title: Rocket Rumble 3D
docs.text:
An optional 2–4-player XZ combat sample for Couch Co-op Builder, Unity 6.3 LTS, URP and Input System. It demonstrates selected-character spawning, isolated actions, profile rebinding, persistent sessions and optional individual cameras. Movement, combat, score and follow behavior are sample-owned; see Player scope for framework capacity.

Figure 5. Rocket Rumble 3D: four assigned views with per-player HUDs. Pause and settings remain global overlays.

docs.title: Open and play
docs.text:
Open RocketRumble3DMainMenu (Assets/LevelArgento/CouchCoopBuilder/Samples/RocketRumble3D/Scenes/RocketRumble3DMainMenu.unity), enter Play Mode and choose PLAY. Join/confirm at least two players, then activate START GAME. First register its three scenes using Configure Supplied Samples. The supplied catalog has Cobalt, Ember, Mint and Orchid, with separate 3D gameplay and preview prefabs. Customize your own copies; keep RocketRumbleShared.

Shared Rocket Rumble guidance explains Audio/Controls settings, Pause, Device Lost, Drop Out/Rejoin and scene returns. Gameplay rebinding leaves lobby/menu controls unchanged.

docs.title: Gameplay controls
docs.text:
Source Move Jump Fire Shield Pause / winner return Keyboard A WASD Space F Left Shift T Keyboard B Arrows Numpad 0 Enter Right Shift Y Gamepad Left stick North South Left Trigger Start Supplied DragonRise profile Profile stick button3 button2 button1 button11

Join/Leave defaults are Q/G, P/Backspace, Start/Select and DragonRise button11/button12. Controls exposes all four keyboard Move directions, Jump, Fire, Shield and Pause / Winner Return; controller rows use vector Move. The sample consumes the framework's profile identity/conflict/reset/storage APIs, described in Input Binding Profiles.

docs.title: Arena, movement and jump
docs.text:
The arena has a 26×22 floor, boundaries, low/middle/high platforms, four indexed initial spawns and twelve safe respawn points. Move projects the shared camera's forward/right onto XZ, clamps diagonal speed to six units/second and retains facing when stopped. Move.y means forward/backward, never Jump.

Jump uses an independent grounded press at velocity 9.3. Per-player airborne acceleration is 2.2 times gravity rising / 3.2 falling; project gravity is unchanged. Approximate floor-jump height is 1.91 units, peak time 0.40 seconds and landing time 0.76 seconds. The 1.2-unit platforms are reachable; 2.8/4.2-unit platforms need intermediate traversal. Grounding accepts floor/platform normals, not side walls. Holding Jump through landing does not repeat it.

Rigidbody/Collider 3D physics, interpolated movement and frozen physical rotation keep presentation facing separate. Player capsules ignore one another; other collisions remain enabled. Rockets ignore their owner, travel horizontally at 20 units/second, expire after three seconds and consume once on hit/block/environment collision. They do not aim, home, splash or arc.

docs.title: Shield, respawn and match
docs.text:
A frontal incoming rocket spends the held Shield without death/score and starts its five-second cooldown; rear/outgoing rockets bypass protection. Raising it leaves movement/fire available; release without a block costs nothing. Death/respawn resets Shield and requires fresh input. HUD shows identity, score, respawn and Shield state.

One unblocked opponent hit awards one attacker point. Ordinary death respawns the same object/context/InputUser after five seconds, retaining selection and score. Twelve authored points use XZ opponent distance: prefer at least six units separation, avoid the previous point when possible, otherwise maximize nearest-opponent separation. Falling below Y=-10 is unscored.

The 3 → 2 → 1 → GO! countdown blocks gameplay. Default first to 10 kills wins; victory freezes gameplay and clears rockets. Any available joined player's Pause shortcut or pointer Return button returns to the originating 3D lobby. Ready and the next match's score reset. Reversible Drop Out releases/recreates the representation while retaining score; Device Lost keeps it. See shared lifecycle guidance.

docs.title: Integration to study
docs.text:
Read the sample's GameplayPlayerSetup (Spawn Selected Character + Explicit Spawn Points), GameplayPlayerBinding (Built-in Actions), 3D player/projectile controllers, match/respawn/HUD components and camera settings integration. The framework owns sessions/users/isolated actions; the game owns combat, scoring, respawn, camera movement and presentation. Shared menus and settings supplies the common authored UI, input profiles and included sample audio.

This game has four authored slots. For an independent 1–8-player camera example, use Split Screen Playgrounds. Neither sample promises camera collision/framing or performance for arbitrary customer levels.

docs.title: Try your integration
docs.text: Join Q/P, confirm and move to Start without clearing Ready. Test independent XZ move/jump/fire/shield, safe respawn and winner return. Use Controls to change a gameplay action while lobby Confirm remains unchanged. Test Pause/Resume, Drop Out/Rejoin and actual Device Lost separately. For cameras, navigate Pause → Camera Settings without mouse; toggle Shared/Split, change 2P/3P layouts, Back and reopen. Repeat with supported controllers and check Console on scene exit.

docs.title: Optional Split Screen cameras
docs.text:
The saved Arena scene includes a GameplayCameraManager with the authored shared camera, an authored player-camera prefab, built-in layouts and the default single AudioListener policy. Split Screen defaults OFF. OFF keeps the original shared 47-degree view and full four-player HUD. ON creates one assigned follow camera per active representation (one to four), plus a compact P#/score/Shield card in each view. Countdown, Pause and Winner remain full-screen overlays.

The follow camera uses GameplayCameraAssignment and its matching GameplayPlayerBinding. It tracks position with a fixed heading inherited from the shared camera, not player facing. Gameplay movement continues to use the shared camera's orientation even while that camera is disabled for rendering. Wide horizontal views use a modestly narrower field of view and lateral arena bias so players stay visible near the edge. There is no orbit, aim camera or collision rig.

During a match, press Pause, navigate to CAMERA SETTINGS using Up/Down, and press Confirm/Submit to open it. Mouse users can click CAMERA SETTINGS on the Pause Card. Focus starts on Split Screen with the menu's orange selection accent. Up/Down selects Split Screen, the visible layout rows, Reset Defaults or Back; Left/Right changes the selected option (or selects a footer button). Confirm activates the focused control. Escape for keyboard roles or the owned controller Back action returns to the Pause menu, as does Back. The authored buttons also support pointer clicks. Resume, Lobby and Main Menu keep their existing pause behavior. Changes apply immediately, including while time is frozen. The 2-player choices are Vertical and Horizontal; the four 3-player choices are Top 2 / Bottom 1, Bottom 2 / Top 1, Left 1 / Right 2, and Right 1 / Left 2. Four players use the framework's 2x2 grid.

Rocket Rumble 3D alone saves these choices under RocketRumble3D.Camera.* using a replaceable IRocketRumble3DCameraPreferences adapter backed by PlayerPrefs. Reset Defaults restores OFF, Vertical and Top 2 / Bottom 1. Camera preferences are sample settings, separate from input binding profiles and the generic camera API. To customize the integration, edit the saved GameplayCameraManager, player-camera prefab and Camera Settings controls in your own copy of the sample.

A camera follows a respawned player without changing its session or owned input. Device loss retains the assigned view while Pause waits for recovery. Intentional Drop Out removes the view; the remaining cameras retile without changing their P# identities. Rejoin restores the reserved view.
